title: Book 6, Chapter 19 — Seventeenth Year of the War—Parties at Syracuse—Story of Harmodius and Aristogiton—Disgrace of Alcibiades
paragraphs: In Syracuse, meanwhile, reports of the expedition arrived from many quarters, but for a long time nobody believed them at all. An assembly was held, and different orators spoke, as will be seen, some trusting the report of the Athenian expedition and some contradicting it. Among them Hermocrates, son of Hermon, came forward. He was convinced that he knew the truth of the matter, and he gave the following counsel:

“Perhaps I shall be no better believed than others have been when I speak about the reality of the expedition. I know that men who make or repeat statements thought unworthy of belief win no converts and are thought fools for their trouble. Still, I shall not be frightened into silence when the state is in danger, and when I am convinced that I can speak on this matter with more authority than other people. You may wonder at it, but the Athenians have indeed set out against us with a large force, naval and military. They claim to be helping the Egestaeans and restoring Leontini, but their real aim is to conquer Sicily, and above all our city; once that is gained, they think, the rest will easily follow. Make up your minds, therefore, to see them here soon, and consider how best to repel them with the means you have at hand. Do not be taken off your guard by despising the news, and do not neglect the common weal by disbelieving it. Meanwhile, those who believe me need not be dismayed by the force or daring of the enemy. They will not be able to hurt us more than we hurt them, and the size of their armament is not wholly a disadvantage to us. On the contrary, the larger it is, the better it is for our position with the rest of the Siceliots, whom dismay will make more ready to join us. And if we defeat them or drive them away, disappointed in their ambition (for I do not fear for a moment that they will get what they want), it will be a most glorious exploit for us, and in my judgment by no means an unlikely one. Few large armaments, Hellenic or barbarian, have gone far from home and succeeded. The invaders cannot outnumber the people of the country and their neighbors, who will all join together out of fear. And if they fail for want of supplies in a foreign land, they still leave renown to the people against whom their plans were laid, even though they may themselves have been the main cause of their own distress. Thus these very Athenians rose to greatness through the defeat of the Mede, which was due in large part to accident, and came merely from the fact that Athens had been the object of his attack. The same may very well happen to us.

“Let us therefore begin our preparations here with confidence. Let us send to some of the Sicels to confirm them, and win the friendship and alliance of others. Let us dispatch envoys to the rest of Sicily to show that the danger is common to all, and to Italy to get its cities to become our allies, or at any rate to refuse to receive the Athenians. I also think it would be best to send to Carthage as well. The Carthaginians are by no means free of apprehension; they live in constant fear that the Athenians may one day attack their city, and they may perhaps think that they themselves would suffer if Sicily were sacrificed. They may be willing to help us secretly if not openly, in one way if not in another. If they will, they are better able to do so than anyone alive today, since they possess the most gold and silver, by which war, like everything else, flourishes. Let us also send to Lacedaemon and Corinth, and ask them to come here and help us as soon as possible, and to keep the war in Hellas alive. But the one thing above all others that I believe we should do at this moment is something that you, with your constitutional love of quiet, will be slow to see, and that I must nevertheless mention. Suppose we Siceliots, all together, or at least as many as possible besides ourselves, were to launch our whole actual navy with two months’ provisions and meet the Athenians at Tarentum and the Iapygian promontory. Suppose we showed them that before fighting for Sicily they must first fight for their passage across the Ionian Sea. We should strike dismay into their army and set them thinking that we have a base for our defensive, since Tarentum is ready to receive us, while they have a wide sea to cross with all their armament. That armament could hardly keep its order through so long a voyage, and since it would come on slowly and in small detachments, it would be easy for us to attack. On the other hand, suppose they lightened their vessels, drew together their fast sailers, and attacked us with these. Then we could fall upon them when they were wearied with rowing, or, if we did not choose to do so, we could retire to Tarentum. They, having crossed with few provisions merely to give battle, would be hard put to it in desolate places. They would have either to remain and be blockaded, or to try to sail along the coast, abandoning the rest of their armament; and they would be further discouraged by not knowing for certain whether the cities would receive them. In my opinion this consideration alone would be enough to deter them from putting out from Corcyra. While they deliberated and reconnoitered our numbers and whereabouts, they would let the season run on until winter was upon them. Or, confounded by so unexpected a circumstance, they would break up the expedition, especially as their most experienced general, as I hear, has taken the command against his will, and would grasp at the first excuse offered by any serious demonstration of ours. We should also be reported, I am certain, as more numerous than we really are. Men’s minds are affected by what they hear; besides, those who are first to attack, or to show that they mean to defend themselves against an attack, inspire greater fear, because men see that they are ready for the emergency. This would be just the case with the Athenians at present. They are attacking us in the belief that we shall not resist, thinking they have a right to judge us severely because we did not help the Lacedaemonians in crushing them. But if they were to see us show a courage for which they are not prepared, they would be more dismayed by the surprise than they could ever be by our actual power. I could wish to persuade you to show this courage. But if that cannot be, at all events lose not a moment in preparing generally for the war. Remember, all of you, that contempt for an assailant is best shown by bravery in action, but that for the present the best course is to accept the preparations that fear inspires as the surest promise of safety, and to act as if the danger were real. That the Athenians are coming to attack us, that they are already on the voyage, and that they are all but here: of this I am sure.”

So spoke Hermocrates. Meanwhile the people of Syracuse were in great strife among themselves. Some insisted that the Athenians had no idea of coming and that there was no truth in what he said. Others asked what harm the Athenians could do, if they did come, that would not be repaid them tenfold. Others made light of the whole affair and turned it into ridicule. In short, few believed Hermocrates and feared for the future. Then Athenagoras, the leader of the people and at that time very powerful with the masses, came forward and spoke as follows:

“Anyone who does not hope that the Athenians are as misguided as they are said to be, and that they will come here to become our subjects, is a coward or a traitor to his country. As for the men who bring us such tidings and fill you with so much alarm, their folly astonishes me more than their audacity, if they imagine we cannot see through them. They have private reasons for fear. They want to throw the city into consternation, so that the public alarm will cast their own terrors into the shade. That, in short, is what these reports are worth. They do not arise of themselves; they are concocted by men who are forever stirring up agitation here in Sicily. But if you are well advised, you will not calculate probabilities from what these persons tell you. You will calculate from what shrewd and experienced men would be likely to do, and that is what I esteem the Athenians to be. It is not likely that they would leave the Peloponnesians at their back, and, before the war in Hellas is properly ended, wantonly go looking for a new war in Sicily that is quite as arduous. In my judgment they are only too glad that we, with so many great cities, do not go and attack them.

“Still, suppose they do come as is reported. I consider that Sicily is better able than Peloponnese to see the war through, because it is better prepared at every point. Our city alone is far more than a match for this pretended army of invasion, even if the army were twice its size. I know that they will bring no horses and will get none here, apart from a few perhaps from the Egestaeans. Nor can they bring heavy infantry equal in number to ours, in ships that will already have enough to do to make the whole journey, however lightly laden. And there is the further transport of the other stores needed against a city of this size, which will be no small quantity. So strong is my opinion on this that I hardly see how they could escape annihilation, even if they brought a second city as large as Syracuse, settled down on our frontier and made war from there. Much less can they hope to succeed with all Sicily hostile to them, as all Sicily will be, and with nothing but a camp set up from the ships, made of tents and bare necessaries, from which fear of our cavalry would keep them from straying far.

“The Athenians see this just as I tell you. They are, as I have reason to know, looking after their possessions at home, while persons here make up stories that are not true and never will be. I have seen these same persons before. When they cannot act, they try by such stories, and by others still more abominable, to frighten your people and seize the government: I see it every time. And I cannot help fearing that, by trying so often, they may one day succeed. So long as we feel no pain, we may prove too weak to prevent it, or, when the offenders are known, to pursue them. The result is that our city is seldom at rest. She suffers constant troubles and as many contests against herself as against the enemy, not to mention occasional tyrannies and infamous cabals. I shall try, however, if you support me, to let none of this happen in our time. I shall win you, the many, and I shall chastise the authors of such machinations. I shall punish them not merely when they are caught in the act, which is difficult, but also for what they wish to do though they lack the power. An enemy must be punished beforehand for what he intends as well as for what he does, if the first to relax precaution is not to be the first to suffer. I shall also reprove, watch, and on occasion warn the few, which I think the most effectual way of turning them from their evil courses. And after all, as I have often asked, what do you want, young men? To hold office at once? The law forbids it. That law was made because you are not competent, not to disgrace you when you are. Meanwhile you would not stand on a legal equality with the many! But how can it be right that citizens of one state should be thought unworthy of the same privileges?

“Perhaps it will be said that democracy is neither wise nor equitable, and that men of property are also the best fitted to rule. My answer is the opposite. First, the word demos, or people, covers the whole state, whereas oligarchy covers only a part. Next, if the rich are the best guardians of property and the wise the best counsellors, then none can hear and decide as well as the many. All these talents, taken one by one or together, have their just place in a democracy. An oligarchy, by contrast, gives the many a share of the danger, and, not content with the largest part of the profit, takes and keeps all of it. That is what the powerful and the young among you aspire to, but in a great city they cannot possibly obtain it.

“Even now, foolish men, the most senseless of all the Hellenes that I know, you may still learn wisdom, if the time for repentance has not passed. If you do not see the wickedness of your designs, you are fools. If you do see it and still dare to pursue them, you are the most criminal of men. Even now you may serve the interest of the country, which is the common interest of us all. Consider that when the country prospers, the men of merit in your ranks will have a share, and a larger one than the great mass of your fellow countrymen; but if you have other designs, you run the risk of losing everything. Give up reports like these, for the people know your object and will not put up with it. If the Athenians arrive, this city will repulse them in a manner worthy of itself. We have, besides, generals who will see to the matter. And if none of this is true, as I incline to believe, the city will not be thrown into a panic by your intelligence, nor will it choose you as its rulers and so impose a servitude on itself. The city will look into the matter itself and will judge your words as if they were acts. It will not listen to you and let its liberty be taken away; it will strive to preserve that liberty, by always keeping at hand the means of making itself respected.”

Such were the words of Athenagoras. Then one of the generals rose and stopped any other speaker from coming forward. On the matter in hand he added these words of his own: “It is not well for speakers to utter calumnies against one another, nor for their hearers to entertain them. We should look instead to the intelligence we have received, and see how each man, and the city as a whole, can best prepare to repel the invaders. Even if there is no need, it does no harm for the state to be furnished with horses and arms and all the other insignia of war. We shall undertake to see to this and give the orders, and to send round to the cities to reconnoiter and do whatever else seems desirable. Part of this we have already seen to, and whatever we discover shall be laid before you.” After these words from the general, the Syracusans left the assembly.

By now the Athenians and all their allies had reached Corcyra. There the generals first reviewed the armament again. They arranged the order in which the ships were to anchor and encamp, and they divided the whole fleet into three divisions, giving one to each of their number. Sailing all together would leave them embarrassed for water, harborage, or provisions at the stations where they touched; with a commander for each squadron, the fleet would also be better ordered and easier to handle. Next they sent three ships ahead to Italy and Sicily, to learn which of the cities would receive them. These ships were told to meet the fleet on its way and report before it put in to land.

After this the Athenians weighed anchor from Corcyra and proceeded to cross to Sicily. The armament now consisted of one hundred and thirty-four galleys in all (besides two Rhodian fifty-oared ships). Of these, one hundred were Athenian vessels, sixty of them warships and forty troopships, and the remainder came from Chios and the other allies. There were five thousand and one hundred heavy infantry in all: fifteen hundred Athenian citizens from the rolls at Athens, seven hundred Thetes shipped as marines, and the rest allied troops, some of them Athenian subjects. Besides these there were five hundred Argives and two hundred and fifty Mantineans serving for hire. There were four hundred and eighty archers in all, eighty of them Cretans; seven hundred slingers from Rhodes; one hundred and twenty light-armed exiles from Megara; and one horse-transport carrying thirty horses.

That was the strength of the first armament that sailed over for the war. Its supplies were carried by thirty ships of burden laden with corn, carrying bakers, stone-masons, and carpenters, along with the tools for building fortifications. A hundred boats, pressed into service like the ships, went with them, and many other boats and ships of burden followed the armament of their own accord, to trade. All of these now left Corcyra and struck out together across the Ionian Sea. The whole force reached land at the Iapygian promontory and Tarentum, with varying fortune, and coasted along the shores of Italy. The cities shut their markets and gates against them and gave them nothing but water and leave to anchor; Tarentum and Locri refused even that. So they came to Rhegium, the extreme point of Italy. There at last they reunited. They were not admitted within the walls, so they pitched a camp outside the city in the precinct of Artemis, where a market was provided for them, drew their ships on shore, and kept quiet. Meanwhile they opened negotiations with the Rhegians, calling on them as Chalcidians to assist their Leontine kinsmen. The Rhegians replied that they would side with neither party, but would wait for the decision of the rest of the Italiots and do as they did. The Athenians then began to consider the best course to take in the affairs of Sicily. In the meantime they waited for the ships sent ahead to return from Egesta, so as to learn whether the money mentioned by the messengers at Athens was really there.

In the meantime positive tidings came in to the Syracusans from all quarters, including their own officers sent to reconnoiter, that the fleet was at Rhegium. They then laid aside their incredulity and threw themselves heart and soul into the work of preparation. Guards or envoys, as the case might be, were sent round to the Sicels; garrisons were put into the posts of the Peripoli in the country; horses and arms were reviewed in the city to see that nothing was wanting; and all other steps were taken to prepare for a war that might be upon them at any moment.

Meanwhile the three ships that had been sent ahead came from Egesta to the Athenians at Rhegium with the news that, so far from there being the sums promised, all that could be produced was thirty talents. The generals were not a little disheartened at being disappointed in this way at the outset. They were disheartened also by the refusal of the Rhegians to join the expedition, the people they had first tried to win and had had most reason to count upon, from their relationship to the Leontines and their constant friendship for Athens. If Nicias was prepared for the news from Egesta, his two colleagues were taken completely by surprise. The Egestaeans had resorted to the following stratagem when the first envoys from Athens came to inspect their resources. They took the envoys to the temple of Aphrodite at Eryx and showed them the treasures deposited there: bowls, wine-ladles, censers, and a large number of other pieces of plate. Being of silver, these gave an impression of wealth quite out of proportion to their really small value. They also entertained the ships’ crews privately. They collected all the cups of gold and silver that they could find in Egesta itself, or could borrow in the neighboring Phoenician and Hellenic towns, and each man brought them to the banquets as his own. Since all used pretty nearly the same cups, and a great quantity of plate was shown everywhere, the effect on the Athenian sailors was most dazzling, and made them talk loudly of the riches they had seen when they got back to Athens. These dupes, who had in their turn persuaded the rest, were much blamed by the soldiers when the news got abroad that there was not the money supposed at Egesta.

Meanwhile the generals consulted on what was to be done. The opinion of Nicias was to sail with all the armament to Selinus, the main object of the expedition. If the Egestaeans could provide money for the whole force, they should advise accordingly; but if they could not, they should require the Egestaeans to supply provisions for the sixty ships that they had asked for. They should stay and settle matters between the Egestaeans and the Selinuntines, either by force or by agreement, and then coast past the other cities. After displaying the power of Athens and proving their zeal for their friends and allies, they should sail home again, unless they should have some sudden and unexpected opportunity of serving the Leontines or of bringing over some of the other cities. They should not endanger the state by wasting its home resources.

Alcibiades said that so great an expedition as this must not disgrace itself by leaving without having accomplished anything. Heralds should be sent to all the cities except Selinus and Syracuse, and efforts should be made to turn some of the Sicels from the Syracusans and to win the friendship of others, so as to have corn and troops. They must first gain the Messinese, whose city lay right on the passage and entrance to Sicily and would give the army an excellent harbor and base. Then, once they had brought over the towns and knew who their allies in the war would be, they might at last attack Syracuse and Selinus, unless Selinus came to terms with Egesta and Syracuse stopped opposing the restoration of Leontini.

Lamachus, for his part, said that they should sail straight for Syracuse and fight their battle at once under the walls of the town, while the people were unprepared and the panic was at its height. Every armament, he said, was most terrible at first. If it let time pass without showing itself, men’s courage revived, and when it finally appeared they saw it almost with indifference. If the Athenians attacked suddenly, while Syracuse still trembled at their coming, they had the best chance of winning a victory and of striking complete panic into the enemy. They would do so through the sight of their numbers, which would never look so considerable as now, through the expectation of coming disaster, and above all through the immediate danger of the battle. They might also count on catching many in the fields outside, who did not believe they were coming; and while the enemy was carrying in his property, the army would not lack booty if it sat down in force before the city. The rest of the Siceliots would then be less inclined to ally themselves with the Syracusans, and would join the Athenians without waiting to see which side was stronger. Megara should be their naval station, to fall back on and to attack from: it was uninhabited, and not far from Syracuse by land or by sea.

Having spoken to this effect, Lamachus nevertheless gave his support to the opinion of Alcibiades. Alcibiades then sailed in his own vessel to Messina with proposals of alliance. He had no success: the inhabitants answered that they could not receive him within their walls, but would provide a market outside. He sailed back to Rhegium. As soon as he returned, the generals manned and victualed sixty ships from the whole fleet and coasted to Naxos, leaving the rest of the armament at Rhegium with one of their number. The Naxians received them, and they coasted on to Catana. There a Syracusan party in the town caused the inhabitants to refuse them admittance, and they went on to the river Terias. They bivouacked there, and the next day sailed to Syracuse in single file with all their ships but ten. Those ten they sent ahead into the great harbor, to see whether any fleet was launched and to proclaim by herald from shipboard that the Athenians had come to restore the Leontines to their country, as their allies and kinsmen. Any Leontines in Syracuse, therefore, should leave without fear and join the Athenians, their friends and benefactors. After making this proclamation, and reconnoitering the city, the harbors, and the features of the country that they would have to use as a base of operations in the war, they sailed back to Catana.

The people of Catana held an assembly. They refused to receive the armament, but invited the generals to come in and say what they wanted. While Alcibiades was speaking and the citizens were absorbed in the assembly, the soldiers unnoticed broke down a poorly walled-up postern gate, entered the town, and streamed into the marketplace. The Syracusan party in the town was not at all numerous. As soon as they saw the army inside they took fright and withdrew. The rest voted for an alliance with the Athenians and invited them to bring the rest of their forces from Rhegium. The Athenians then sailed to Rhegium and set out again, this time with all the armament, for Catana, where on arrival they began at once to work on their camp.

Soon afterward word came to them from Camarina that the town would go over to them if they came, and also that the Syracusans were manning a fleet. The Athenians therefore sailed along the coast with all their armament. They went first to Syracuse, where they found no fleet being manned, and then on along the coast to Camarina. They put in at the beach and sent a herald to the people, who refused to receive them. They said that their oaths bound them to receive the Athenians only with a single vessel, unless they themselves sent for more. Disappointed here, the Athenians sailed back. They landed on Syracusan territory and plundered it, and when the Syracusan horse came up they lost some stragglers of their light infantry. Then they returned to Catana.

There they found the Salaminia, which had come from Athens for Alcibiades. Its orders were that he should sail home to answer the charges the state brought against him, and the same for certain other soldiers accused with him of sacrilege in the matter of the mysteries and of the Hermae. Since the expedition left, the Athenians had gone on investigating the mysteries and the Hermae as actively as ever. In their suspicious temper they did not test the informers but welcomed them all alike. On the evidence of rascals they arrested and imprisoned the best citizens. They preferred to sift the matter to the bottom rather than let an accused man of good character go unquestioned because the informer was a rascal. The commons had heard how oppressive the tyranny of Pisistratus and his sons became before it ended, and also that it was put down at last not by themselves and Harmodius but by the Lacedaemonians. So they were always afraid and took everything suspiciously.

The daring act of Aristogiton and Harmodius arose from a love affair. I shall tell it at some length, to show that the Athenians are no more accurate than anyone else in what they say about their own tyrants and their own history. Pisistratus died at an advanced age while still holding the tyranny, and he was succeeded by his eldest son Hippias, not by Hipparchus, as is commonly believed. At that time Harmodius was in the flower of youthful beauty. Aristogiton, a citizen of middle rank, was his lover and had won him. Hipparchus, son of Pisistratus, pursued Harmodius without success. Harmodius told Aristogiton, and the enraged lover feared that the powerful Hipparchus might take Harmodius by force. He at once formed a plan to overthrow the tyranny, as far as his station in life allowed. Meanwhile Hipparchus pursued Harmodius a second time with no better success. He was unwilling to use violence, so he arranged to insult him in some indirect way. In general, indeed, the government of these men was not oppressive to the multitude, nor in any way hateful in practice. These tyrants cultivated wisdom and virtue as much as any rulers did. They exacted no more than a twentieth of the Athenians’ income, yet they splendidly adorned the city, carried on its wars and provided sacrifices for the temples. For the rest, the city kept its existing laws in full enjoyment, except that care was always taken to put the offices in the hands of some member of the family. One of them who held the yearly archonship at Athens was Pisistratus, son of the tyrant Hippias and named after his grandfather. During his term of office he dedicated the altar to the twelve gods in the market-place, and that of Apollo in the Pythian precinct. Later the Athenian people added to the altar in the market-place, lengthening it, and wiped out the inscription. But the one in the Pythian precinct can still be seen, though in faded letters, and it reads as follows:
Pisistratus, the son of Hippias, Sent up this record of his archonship In precinct of Apollo Pythias.

That Hippias was the eldest son and succeeded to the government, I state positively as a fact, since I have had more exact accounts of it than others. It can also be shown by the following circumstance. He is the only one of the legitimate brothers who appears to have had children, as the altar shows, and the pillar set up in the Athenian Acropolis to commemorate the crime of the tyrants. That pillar names no child of Thessalus or of Hipparchus, but five of Hippias, whom he had by Myrrhine, daughter of Callias, son of Hyperechides. It is natural that the eldest would have married first. Again, his name comes first on the pillar after that of his father, and this too is quite natural, since he was the eldest after him and the reigning tyrant. Nor can I ever believe that Hippias would have obtained the tyranny so easily if Hipparchus had been in power when he was killed, and Hippias had had to establish himself on that same day. No doubt he had long been accustomed to overawe the citizens and to be obeyed by his mercenaries. So he not only conquered but conquered with ease, without any of the embarrassment of a younger brother unused to exercising authority. It was the sad fate of Hipparchus that made him famous, and that also gave him, with posterity, the credit of having been tyrant.

To return to Harmodius. Hipparchus, repulsed in his advances, insulted him as he had resolved to do. He first invited a sister of Harmodius, a young girl, to come and carry a basket in a certain procession. Then he rejected her, on the pretext that she had never been invited at all because she was unworthy. Harmodius was indignant at this, and Aristogiton, for his sake, became more exasperated than ever. They arranged everything with those who were to join them in the enterprise, and they waited only for the great feast of the Panathenaea. That was the only day on which the citizens who formed part of the procession could meet together in arms without arousing suspicion. Aristogiton and Harmodius were to begin, and their accomplices were to support them at once against the bodyguard. For greater security the conspirators were not many. They also hoped that those outside the plot would be carried away by the example of a few daring spirits, and would use the arms in their hands to recover their liberty.

At last the festival arrived. Hippias and his bodyguard were outside the city in the Ceramicus, arranging how the different parts of the procession were to move off. Harmodius and Aristogiton already had their daggers and were getting ready to act. Then they saw one of their accomplices talking familiarly with Hippias, who was easy of access to everyone. They took fright and concluded that they had been discovered and were about to be seized. They were eager, if possible, to take revenge first on the man who had wronged them and for whose sake they had undertaken all this risk. So they rushed, just as they were, inside the gates. They met Hipparchus by the Leocorium and fell on him at once without caution, infuriated, Aristogiton by love and Harmodius by insult, and they struck him down and killed him. Aristogiton escaped the guards at that moment, because the crowd was running up, but he was taken afterwards and put to death without mercy. Harmodius was killed on the spot.

When the news was brought to Hippias in the Ceramicus, he did not go to the scene of the deed. He went at once to the armed men in the procession, who were some distance away and knew nothing yet of the matter. He composed his features for the occasion so as not to betray himself, pointed to a certain spot, and ordered them to go there without their arms. They withdrew, imagining he had something to say to them. Then he told the mercenaries to remove the arms, and picked out on the spot the men he thought guilty, and anyone found with a dagger, since the shield and spear were the usual weapons for a procession.

In this way offended love first led Harmodius and Aristogiton to conspire, and the alarm of the moment led them to the rash action I have described. After this the tyranny pressed harder on the Athenians. Hippias, now more fearful, put many of the citizens to death, and at the same time began to look abroad for a refuge in case of revolution. So although he was an Athenian, he gave his daughter Archedice to a Lampsacene, Aeantides, son of the tyrant of Lampsacus, seeing that they had great influence with Darius. Her tomb is in Lampsacus, with this inscription:
Archedice lies buried in this earth, Hippias her sire, and Athens gave her birth; Unto her bosom pride was never known, Though daughter, wife, and sister to the throne.

Hippias reigned three years longer over the Athenians. In the fourth year he was deposed by the Lacedaemonians and the banished Alcmaeonidae. He went under a safe conduct to Sigeum, and to Aeantides at Lampsacus, and from there to King Darius. From the court of Darius he set out twenty years later, in his old age, and came with the Medes to Marathon.

The Athenian people kept these events in mind and recalled everything they knew by hearsay on the subject. They became hard to please and suspicious of the persons charged in the affair of the mysteries, and they were persuaded that all that had taken place was part of an oligarchical and monarchical conspiracy. Irritation ran high, and many persons of consideration had already been thrown into prison. Far from showing any sign of abating, public feeling grew more savage every day, and more arrests were made. At last one of those in custody, who was thought to be the most guilty of all, was persuaded by a fellow prisoner to make a revelation. Whether it was true or not is disputed, for there are two opinions, and no one has been able, either then or since, to say for certain who did the deed. However that may be, the other man found arguments to persuade him that even if he had not done it, he ought to save himself by getting a promise of impunity, and free the state of its present suspicions. He would be surer of safety, he said, if he confessed after a promise of impunity than if he denied it and were brought to trial. So he made a revelation, implicating himself and others in the affair of the Hermae. The Athenian people supposed that they had at last got at the truth. Until then they had been furious at being unable to discover those who had conspired against the commons. Now they at once let go the informer and all the others whom he had not denounced. They brought the accused to trial and executed all who were apprehended, and condemned to death those who had fled, setting a price on their heads. In all this it was, after all, not clear whether the sufferers had been punished unjustly, while in any case the rest of the city received immediate and obvious relief.

To return to Alcibiades. Public feeling was very hostile to him. It was worked on by the same enemies who had attacked him before he left, and now that the Athenians fancied they had got at the truth about the Hermae, they believed more firmly than ever that the affair of the mysteries, in which he was implicated, had been contrived by him with the same intention and was connected with the plot against the democracy. Meanwhile, just at the time of this agitation, it so happened that a small force of Lacedaemonians had advanced as far as the Isthmus, in pursuit of some scheme with the Boeotians. It was now thought that this force had come by appointment, at his instigation, and not on account of the Boeotians. It was thought also that if the citizens had not acted on the information received and forestalled them by arresting the prisoners, the city would have been betrayed. The citizens went so far as to sleep one night under arms in the temple of Theseus within the walls. The friends of Alcibiades at Argos were also suspected, at this very time, of a design to attack the commons. The Argive hostages deposited in the islands were therefore given up by the Athenians to the Argive people to be put to death. In short, everywhere something was found to create suspicion against Alcibiades. It was therefore decided to bring him to trial and execute him. The Salaminia was sent to Sicily for him and the others named in the information, with instructions to order him to come and answer the charges against him, but not to arrest him. The Athenians wished to avoid causing any agitation in the army or among the enemy in Sicily, and above all to keep the services of the Mantineans and Argives, who, it was thought, had been induced to join by his influence. Alcibiades, with his own ship and his fellow accused, sailed away from Sicily with the Salaminia as though to return to Athens. They went with her as far as Thurii, and there they left the ship and disappeared, afraid to go home for trial with such a prejudice against them. The crew of the Salaminia stayed some time looking for Alcibiades and his companions. At length, as they were nowhere to be found, they set sail and departed. Not long after, Alcibiades, now an outlaw, crossed in a boat from Thurii to Peloponnese. The Athenians passed sentence of death by default on him and on those in his company.
